standard_prerequisites.name: Arithmetic of powers in a ring and the description of the powers of an element as a numerical semigroup generated by two consecutive integers
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Used at proof lines 11822-11825, where the identity expressing b to the power (k+i)n+i is written down
standard_prerequisites.use: Shows that all sufficiently large powers of the given element lie in the subring, with the explicit bound n squared.

standard_prerequisites.name: Existence of a largest exponent with the property that the corresponding power does not lie in the subring, using that all large powers do lie in it
standard_prerequisites.use: Produces the element whose square and cube are in the subring.

core_obligations: Make the hypothesis effective: if b to the n and b to the n+1 lie in A, then every power b to the m with m at least n squared lies in A, as the displayed identity with exponents (k+i)n+i shows (proof lines 11822-11825).
Choose the largest exponent i at least one for which b to the i is outside A, which exists because all sufficiently large powers are inside A (proof lines 11826-11827).

Conclude for that element: both twice the exponent i and three times it are at least n squared, hence b to the i squared and b to the i cubed lie in A, which is the asserted element (proof lines 11827-11829).
proof_roadmap: Show that all powers beyond n squared are in the subring, then take the largest exponent still outside and read off the square and cube conditions (proof lines 11822-11829).
difficulty_reason: The lemma says that if a ring extension contains an element outside the subring with two consecutive powers inside it, then it also contains an element outside the subring whose square and cube are inside (statement lines 11813-11820). The counted proof is complete and short: it writes the identity showing that every power of the element with exponent at least n squared lies in the subring, takes the largest exponent whose power is still outside, and observes that twice and three times that exponent exceed n squared, which gives the required element (proof lines 11822-11829). It is H2: the argument is an elementary numerical observation carried out in the counted span, and its value for the surrounding seminormality theory is as a reduction step.
